meaning: 'Great heaven' (Māori rangi 'sky, heavens' + nui 'great'), the sky father prised apart from the earth mother Papatūānuku by their children.

phonemes.desc: Alveolar tap [ɾ] as in Spanish 'pero', followed by open [a] — the name begins with a lightly tapped syllable.
Velar nasal [ŋ], the sound in English 'singer', followed by short [i].
[nui] 'great' — [n] with the falling diphthong [ui], 'oo-ee' said quickly.

pronunciation.approximation: 'RAH-ngi-NOO-ee' — tap the 'r' as in Spanish 'pero'; 'ng' is the sound in 'singer'; the four light syllables run together.

kin.label: Māori
kin.form: Rangi, 'sky, heavens' + nui, 'great' — 'Great Heaven' (Williams, A Dictionary of the Māori Language, s.v. rangi, nui).

kin.label: Hawaiian
kin.form: Wākea, the sky father paired with Papahānaumoku — the Polynesian cognate pair (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology).

kin.label: Tahitian
kin.form: ra'i, the Polynesian cognate of rangi (Tregear, The Māori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary, s.v. rangi).

pronunciation.note: The form Ranginui is plain ASCII — Māori writes this name with no diacritics — so the restoration recovers nothing but the capital that marks a proper name, and the name stands at Tier 2 by the mechanical rule. Its authenticity needs no orthographic argument: the name has been transmitted without break in Māori oral and ceremonial tradition.

domains.title: Ranginui
domains.subtitle: Sky
domains.lead: Ranginui is the sky father of Māori cosmogony — rangi, 'sky', with nui, 'great'. He and the earth mother Papatūānuku lay locked in an embrace that left the world in darkness, until their children forced them apart so that light, and humanity, could live between them. He is separation and longing: the rain is his tears, the mist her sighs, and the space between sky and earth the world we inhabit.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: Rangi 'sky' + nui 'great': Great Heaven, the primordial sky father of Māori cosmogony (Williams, Dictionary of the Māori Language).

cards.name: Sky
cards.desc: The primordial sky locked in darkness with the earth mother Papatūānuku until their children prised them apart.

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: The separation of Rangi and Papa is the founding story of the Māori world, still told on every marae and carved into every wharenui.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Honored as a flagship temple; the Māori form needs no diacritics, so the restoration is the scholarly citation form, capitalization and all.

symbols.name: Rain
symbols.meaning: The tears of Rangi falling on Papatūānuku — the sky father's enduring grief at the separation (Grey, Polynesian Mythology).

symbols.name: Mist
symbols.meaning: The sighs of Papatūānuku rising to meet him — the parents' continuing dialogue written on the morning air (Orbell, Māori Myth and Legend).

symbols.name: The ridge-pole (tahuhu)
symbols.meaning: In the wharenui the ridge-beam is Rangi held above the earth floor, Papa: every meeting house re-enacts the separation.

symbols.name: The stars
symbols.meaning: The children hung in the sky by Tāne to give their father light and to adorn his darkness (White, Ancient History of the Māori).

mythology.lead: Ranginui's mythology is Māori cosmogony itself, as recorded by Sir George Grey and John White from oral tradition in the nineteenth century: the primordial embrace, the separation, and the war among the children that followed. It is a living narrative — still told on marae, still carved into meeting houses — and it explains the visible world: rain, mist, storm, and the light between sky and earth.

myths.title: The Embrace of Rangi and Papa
myths.text: In the beginning the sky father Ranginui and the earth mother Papatūānuku clung together in an embrace that knew no end, and in the darkness between their bodies their children were born — seventy sons in the telling recorded by Grey in Polynesian Mythology (1854). There was no light: the world was the cramped hollow of the parents' clasp, and the children grew hemmed in on every side, some of them longing for room and for brightness, others content in the warm dark. The myth opens not with a bang but with an embrace, and its first claim is psychological before it is cosmological — love so complete that it suffocates: the parents' happiness is the children's captivity, and creation cannot begin until something beloved breaks.

myths.title: Tāne Pushes the Sky Away
myths.text: The children argued over how to win light. Tūmatauenga, the fierce one, proposed killing the parents — a plan the others rejected with horror. Then Tāne, the resourceful one, lay on his back between them and, bracing his head against the earth and his feet against the sky, pushed (Grey; White, Ancient History of the Māori). Ranginui cried out in agony as he was lifted, and Papatūānuku groaned beneath him, still clinging, her torn body leaving the marks of her grief in the hills and valleys of the earth. Alone among the brothers, Tāwhirimāteā, lord of winds, sided with his father and withdrew in rage to the sky. The separation is the Māori account of why there is a world at all: light, space, and death itself enter existence in the moment the divided parents grieve — the world begins as an act of necessary violence against love.

myths.title: Why the Sky Weeps
myths.text: The parents never resigned themselves to the parting, and the tradition reads the weather as their continuing grief. The rain that falls from Ranginui is his tears of longing for Papatūānuku; the mist that rises from her breast is her sighs, drifting up to meet him (Grey; Orbell, Māori Myth and Legend). In some tellings the pale bloom on the riverbanks of harakeke, the New Zealand flax, marks where the tears of the pair fell thickest. The myth makes weather into emotion: every downpour and every soft morning fog is the conversation of the divided lovers — a cosmos that is not machinery but kinship, still grieving, still in love, and entirely unashamed of either.

myths.title: Tāwhirimāteā's Revenge
myths.text: Tāwhirimāteā, who alone had opposed the separation, took his grieving father into the sky and made war on his brothers. He gouged out the eyes of Tangaroa's children — the fish and the crawling things of the sea, which is why the sea's creatures hide in the deep — and he hurled his winds and storms against Tāne's forests, snapping the trees. Tūmatauenga stood against him and won, and the winds were driven up into the fatherless sky (Grey; Best, Māori Religion and Mythology). The war among the children is the myth's hardest lesson: the act that creates the world also divides it. Harmony among the forces of nature is never given — it was fought for once, and it must be remade continually, which is why the winds still test the trees.

myths.title: Tāne Hangs the Lights
myths.text: Left alone in the high darkness, Ranginui needed light, and Tāne set the stars in the body of his father. In the traditions recorded by White, the stars are children of the sky hung as lamps to adorn him, and among them are the navigational stars by which the ancestors steered their canoes across the Pacific to Aotearoa. The crowning act of the separation is not punishment but decoration: Tāne, who pushed his parents apart, gives his father the stars as compensation. The night sky thus carries the story in its own substance — the sky father's beauty is his children's doing, and the lights by which humans find their way across the ocean are a family's peace offering to its father, hung where the whole world can steer by it.

lore.syncretism: Ranginui is the Māori face of the Polynesian sky father, whose other avatars include the Hawaiian Wākea — the sky paired with Papahānaumoku, whose very name repeats the Papa of Māori tradition (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology) — and the Tahitian and Rarotongan ra'i and rangi of cognate cosmogonies; the separation of a primordial parental pair recurs across the Pacific. Nineteenth-century European recorders, Grey among them, were quick to hear biblical echoes — a sky father, an earth mother, children thrust out of a dark paradise — and Māori Christianity in turn folded Rangi and Papa into a theology of creation that could be preached from the pulpit. The carved meeting house became the permanent site of the synthesis: its ridge-pole is Rangi, its floor Papa, its ancestors the children between them. Later Māori thought, including the contested twentieth-century traditions gathered around the god Io, debated whether the sky father pointed toward a single supreme being; the scholarly consensus treats the separation myth as the genuine core and the monotheistic framing as accretion (Orbell).
lore.culturalLegacy: The separation of Ranginui and Papatūānuku remains the founding narrative of Māori identity — taught in schools, sung in waiata, and carved into the wharenui of every marae, where the building itself is the myth: ridge-pole as sky, floor as earth, ancestors as the space between. The national museum of New Zealand takes its name, Te Papa Tongarewa, from the earth mother of his embrace. Rangi is a living given name, and the pair have travelled far beyond Aotearoa: the story appears in environmental theology, indigenous-rights discourse, and the global revival of creation narratives as title-deeds of belonging. And the rain-as-tears reading gives Māori weather its poetry and its pedagogy — the landscape is a family, and the family is still speaking.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ranginui is the god of necessary grief. The myth refuses the fantasy that love alone could sustain the world: the parents' perfect embrace is a prison for their children, and the world begins only when Tāne's legs force the lovers apart. What the story understands — with a psychological precision rare among cosmogonies — is that separation is not the failure of love but its condition. Rangi and Papa do not stop loving each other: the rain is his tears, the mist her sighs, and the whole weather of the world is their continuing conversation.

To meditate on Ranginui is to meditate on every necessary leaving — the child who must push away the parents in order to stand up, the people who must leave the homeland to become themselves. The children win light and space, but they inherit a wound, and the father's grief falls on them daily as rain. The Māori genius is to make that wound sacred rather than tragic: the tears water the flax, the mist feeds the morning, and the sky, for all its weeping, holds the stars.
lore.archaeology: Māori tradition built no temples, so Ranginui's archaeology is the archaeology of the meeting house: the great carved wharenui of the nineteenth century are material cosmogonies. Te Hau-ki-Tūranga (carved c. 1842, now at Te Papa Tongarewa) shows the convention fully formed — the tahuhu ridge-pole as the sky father, the earth floor as Papatūānuku, and the carved ancestors standing between them. The textual witnesses are themselves artifacts: Grey recorded the separation cycle from Māori informants in Nga Mahi a nga Tupuna (1854), and White's Ancient History of the Māori (1887–90) preserved variants from the Tainui and Te Arawa traditions. Earlier than both stands the transmission they committed to paper — an unbroken oral and ceremonial custody, measured in centuries, that no excavation is needed to prove.
